Adjetivo sem artigo, passo a passo: Adjectives with no article, step by step
PASSO 1: sem artigo (nem der, nem ein),: STEP 1: with no article (neither der nor ein), the ADJECTIVE has to show the case ALL BY ITSELF. STEP 2: it borrows the endings of the definite article: «der» → -er, «die» → -e, «das» → -es, plural «die» → -e. STEP 3: nominative: kalter Kaffee (m), kalte Milch (f), kaltes Wasser (n), kalte Getränke (plural). STEP 4: accusative: as always, only the masculine changes: kalten Kaffee (-en); the rest is the same as the nominative. STEP 5: you'll use this with UNCOUNTABLE nouns (Kaffee, Milch, Wasser, Brot, Obst), with PLURALS without an article (gute Freunde — good friends), and in orders and prices: «Ich möchte kalten Kaffee» (I'd like iced coffee), «Wir haben frisches Brot» (we have fresh bread).
o português diz «café frio», «água gelad: English says "cold coffee", "fresh bread", "good friends" without a second thought. These are exactly the cases where German has no article — so the adjective must carry the case with the endings of «der, die, das»: kalter Kaffee, frisches Brot, gute Freunde.

PASSO 1: no DATIVO, sem artigo, as termi: STEP 1: in the DATIVE, with no article, the endings are: -em (m), -er (f), -em (n), -en (plural) — again the endings of dem, der, dem, den: «mit kaltem Kaffee», «mit kalter Milch», «mit kaltem Wasser», «mit kalten Getränken». STEP 2: after «viele» (many), «wenige» (few), «einige» (some), «mehrere» (several), the adjective also takes the no-article ending: «viele neue Bücher», «einige gute Freunde». STEP 3: after «alle» (all), the adjective takes «-en», as after «die»: «alle neuen Bücher». STEP 4: use the no-article form to talk about people or things in general: «Ich esse gern frisches Obst» (I like eating fresh fruit).

As três famílias em um só quadro: The three families in one chart
PASSO 1: o alemão quer o caso UMA vez só: STEP 1: German wants the case shown ONCE: either on the article or on the adjective. STEP 2: with DER/DIE/DAS (the article shows the case): the adjective takes «-e» or «-en». STEP 3: with EIN/MEIN/KEIN (the article doesn't show the case in the masculine nominative and in the neuter): the adjective takes «-er» and «-es» there, and «-e/-en» everywhere else. STEP 4: with NO article: the adjective shows the case with the endings of «der, die, das» (and dem in the dative). STEP 5: memory trick: "If the article fails, the adjective takes over."
